question: I think one of the things that makes Re:Zero so interesting is the weakness and growth of its characters. In particular, I think the way Subaru's emotions change is wonderfully portrayed—he sheds his early immaturity, then gets knocked down again, and so on. Is there any trick or approach you use when it comes to understanding a character's emotions within the story?
answer:
I suppose it's “humanity.”

I think people change over time.

If you look at someone simply as a “character,” I think there's a tendency to fix them into a certain mold or develop a predetermined understanding of them. But when I'm writing my own work and put myself in the character's perspective, things like, “This is how they felt in this scene. And this is the reason they came to feel that way,” gradually build up—the emotional flow, episodes, and history of that person as a human being.

If you're depicting human beings, it's only natural that there are good days and bad days. There are days when you're feeling motivated and days when you're not, days when your work progresses and days when it doesn't. I think it's about those kinds of fluctuations.

In the actual story, those things become somewhat more exaggerated and event-like, but if you keep doing that, you end up depicting a human being as a result. I think that's what comes through in Subaru and the other characters as well.
